subtopics.title: VHDL Overview, Structure & Data Types
subtopics.subtitle: What VHDL is, the design flow, entity/architecture, port modes and core data types

concepts.text: Why a Hardware Description Language

VHDL stands for VHSIC Hardware Description Language, where VHSIC is Very High Speed Integrated Circuit, a US Department of Defense programme of the 1980s. It is standardised as IEEE 1076 (revisions 1987, 1993, 2002, 2008). Unlike a software language, VHDL describes hardware that operates concurrently, and the same description is used both to simulate a design and to synthesise it into gates for an FPGA or ASIC. Verilog (IEEE 1364, now SystemVerilog IEEE 1800) is the other major HDL, with a terser C-like syntax.
Typical HDL design flow:
items: Specification: define function, interfaces and timing targets.
HDL coding (RTL): write entities and architectures in VHDL.
Functional simulation: a testbench applies stimulus and checks outputs, no timing yet.
Synthesis: the tool maps RTL to a gate-level netlist of the target library or FPGA primitives.
Implementation: place and route (FPGA) or floorplan, placement and routing (ASIC), followed by static timing analysis.
Timing simulation and sign-off, then programming the FPGA bitstream or ASIC fabrication.

concepts.text: Design Units: Library, Entity, Architecture

A VHDL file usually begins with library ieee; and use clauses such as use ieee.std_logic_1164.all; to make standard types visible. The entity declares the external interface: its name, ports and optional generics. The architecture body describes what happens inside, and one entity may have several architectures. A package collects shared types, constants, functions and components, and a configuration binds an entity to a chosen architecture (or component instances to specific entities).

concepts.text: The three architecture (modelling) styles:
items: Behavioural: describes what the circuit does using processes with if, case and loops, e.g. a process that compares two inputs.
Dataflow: describes how data flows using concurrent signal assignments and Boolean equations, e.g. s <= a xor b.
Structural: builds the design by instantiating and wiring components with port map, like a schematic netlist.
Real designs mix styles: a top level is often structural, while leaf blocks are dataflow or behavioural.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: VHDL Semantics, Types and Attributes

A VHDL simulator works in cycles: each triggered process runs until it reaches a wait statement (or the end of a process with a sensitivity list), and only then are the scheduled signal values updated, one delta cycle later at the same simulation time. Every signal read during one run of a process therefore sees the old value, and when the same signal is assigned twice in one run the last assignment wins. Variables change at once, and a process's variables keep their values from one activation of the process to the next (variables declared in a subprogram are re-created on every call). At time zero every object without an explicit initial value starts at the leftmost value of its type, T'left: 'U' for std_logic, the first literal of an enumeration, 0 for natural and integer'left for integer.
Type rules that often trip up beginners:
items: VHDL is strongly typed: std_logic_vector, unsigned and signed are distinct types, so an unsigned result must be converted back with std_logic_vector(...), and a vector becomes a number only through to_integer(unsigned(...)).

A subtype such as natural, positive or integer range 0 to 255 is compatible with its base type, and a value outside its range is a run-time bound-check error, never a silent wrap-around; a type declared with type t is range ... is a new type that needs an explicit conversion.
Array assignments must match in length: VHDL never pads or truncates automatically, so a 7-element value assigned to an 8-element target is an error.
Aggregates build composite values by position or by name, e.g. (7 => '1', others => '0') for a 7 downto 0 vector sets only its leftmost bit, and others fills whatever remains.
Bit-string literals: X"3C" is 00111100 and O"17" is 001111; VHDL-2008 allows a width prefix, and without a signed specifier the value is zero-extended on the left.
Record fields are selected with a dot (p.r, p.g) and array elements with parentheses, so mem(3)(7) is bit 7 of word 3 of an array of vectors.

rows: Bounds as written; for an ascending range 'left is the low bound
The index range, reusable in loops and declarations

concepts.text: Operator rules worth memorising:
items: and, or, xor, nand, nor and xnor have equal precedence, so mixing them needs parentheses: a and b or c does not compile while a and b and c does, and nand or nor cannot be chained at all.
not binds more tightly than the binary logical operators, so not a and b means (not a) and b.
Integer / truncates toward zero, rem takes the sign of the left operand and mod takes the sign of the right operand: 7 rem (−3) = 1 but 7 mod (−3) = −2.
Unary minus has lower precedence than *, /, mod and rem, so −7 mod 3 is read as −(7 mod 3) = −1; write (−7) mod 3 when a negative operand is meant.

The predefined relational operators on std_logic_vector compare element by element from the left, like strings, and vectors of different lengths are never equal; convert to unsigned or signed for a numeric comparison.
& concatenates elements and arrays, so for a 4-bit a, a(2 downto 0) & '0' shifts left by one place and a(0) & a(3 downto 1) rotates right.

concepts.text: Rules for concurrent statements and processes:
items: Concurrent statements (signal assignments, when-else, with-select, processes and instances) run whenever their inputs change, so their order in the architecture does not matter; if, case and loop are sequential and belong inside a process or subprogram.

In when-else the first true condition wins, giving a priority structure; with-select and case must cover every value of the selector, and since std_logic has nine values a 2-element std_logic_vector has 9² = 81 values, so when others is needed.

A process has either a sensitivity list or wait statements, never both; an incomplete sensitivity list makes simulation differ from the synthesised logic, and VHDL-2008 process (all) avoids the problem.
y <= a after 5 ns uses inertial delay, which swallows pulses shorter than 5 ns, while transport delay passes every pulse; synthesis ignores after clauses.
clk'event and clk = '1' is also true for a change from 'U' or 'X' to '1', whereas rising_edge(clk) additionally requires the previous value to be '0' or 'L'.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: reading a signal in the same process run that assigns it and expecting the new value; leaving inputs out of a combinational process's sensitivity list; using the non-standard std_logic_arith or std_logic_unsigned packages instead of numeric_std; comparing std_logic_vector values with < or > and expecting a numeric result; driving one std_logic signal from two processes, which resolves to 'X' when they disagree; and forgetting when others in a case or with-select on a std_logic_vector.

notes.text: Entity = interface (ports), architecture = implementation. MCQs often test the nine std_logic values, especially 'Z' (high impedance), 'X' (unknown) and 'U' (uninitialised).
Signals use <= and update only after the process suspends; variables use := and update immediately. Reading a signal just after assigning it in the same process returns the old value.
VHDL is not case sensitive, comments start with --, and every statement ends with a semicolon.

flashcards.front: What do the entity and the architecture describe in VHDL?
flashcards.back: The entity declares the interface (name, ports, generics); the architecture describes the internal behaviour or structure.

flashcards.front: Name the three VHDL modelling styles.
flashcards.back: Behavioural (processes), dataflow (concurrent assignments) and structural (component instantiation with port map).

flashcards.front: How does a signal differ from a variable in VHDL?
flashcards.back: A signal (<=) updates after a delta cycle and is visible across the architecture; a variable (:=) updates immediately and is local to its process.

questions.questionText: Which std_logic value represents the high-impedance state used for tri-state buses?
questions.explanation: 'Z' is high impedance. 'X' is forcing unknown, 'U' is uninitialised and '-' is don't care.

questions.questionText: Inside a VHDL process, when does a variable assignment (v := a + 1;) take effect?
options: Immediately, so the next statement sees the new value
At the next rising clock edge
questions.explanation: Variables update immediately. Signal assignments are the ones scheduled for after the process suspends (one delta cycle later).

questions.questionText: Under which IEEE standard number is VHDL standardised?
questions.explanation: VHDL is IEEE 1076, first standardised in 1987 and revised in 1993, 2000, 2002, 2008 and 2019. IEEE 1364 is Verilog, 1800 is SystemVerilog and 754 is floating-point arithmetic.
v changes at once, but s <= 5 is only scheduled and takes effect after the process suspends, so the first report prints 0 5. After wait for 1 ns the second report prints 5 5.

options: y becomes "01010011" because the value is zero-extended on the left
y becomes "10100110" because the value is left-justified
y becomes "U1010011", with the unassigned bit left uninitialised
An error is reported because the 7-element value does not fit the 8-element target
questions.explanation: a & b has 4 + 3 = 7 elements and VHDL never pads or truncates in an array assignment; GHDL stops with a bound-check failure. Writing '0' & a & b makes the lengths match and gives "01010011".

Inside the loop acc still reads its old value 0, so the four assignments schedule 1, 2, 3 and 4 in turn and only the last survives; after the wait acc = 4, as GHDL reports. A variable would have accumulated 10.

questions.questionText: Which VHDL design unit selects the architecture used for an entity, or the entity bound to each component instance, without editing the design itself?
questions.explanation: A configuration declaration binds entities to architectures and component instances to entities. Without one, an entity instantiated with no architecture name uses its most recently analysed architecture.

questions.questionText: For signal v : std_logic_vector(2 to 9);, what are v'left, v'right and v'length?
questions.explanation: 'left and 'right are the bounds as written, so for this ascending range 'left = 2 and 'right = 9, and 'length = 9 − 2 + 1 = 8. For a downto range 'left would be the high bound.

questions.questionText: Which VHDL design unit collects type declarations, constants, functions and component declarations so that several designs can share them through a use clause?
questions.explanation: A package, with an optional package body holding subprogram code, is analysed into a library and made visible with a clause such as use work.my_pkg.all;. Declarations inside an architecture are visible only in that architecture.

questions.questionText: Given type state_t is (IDLE, LOAD, RUN, DONE);, what is state_t'pos(RUN)?
options: Undefined, because 'pos applies only to integer types
questions.explanation: Enumeration literals are numbered from 0 in declaration order, so IDLE = 0, LOAD = 1 and RUN = 2, as GHDL reports. 'pos, 'val, 'succ and 'pred all apply to enumeration types.
Record fields are selected with a dot after the object name. GHDL rejects p(g) and g.p because no object named g exists, and p'g because ' introduces an attribute.

Each object starts at T'left, the leftmost value of its subtype: natural'left = 0, the range 5 to 20 starts at 5, and IDLE is the first enumeration literal (GHDL reports n=0 r=5 st=idle). 'U' is the default only for types based on std_ulogic.

questions.questionText: A VHDL design unit has no library or use clauses at all. Which of these types can it still use?
questions.explanation: Every design unit implicitly has library std, work; and use std.standard.all;, which declares bit, boolean, integer, character, string and time. std_logic and std_logic_vector need ieee.std_logic_1164 and unsigned needs ieee.numeric_std; GHDL reports 'no declaration' for them.

questions.questionText: A synthesis tool implements signal count : integer range 0 to 999; as an unsigned binary number. How many bits does it need?
questions.explanation: ceil(log2(999 + 1)) = ceil(9.97) = 10 bits, because 2^9 = 512 is too small and 2^10 = 1024 is enough; GHDL --synth maps the port to a 10-bit vector. An unconstrained integer would take 32 bits.

questions.questionText: Which port mode suits a data-bus pin that the entity must both drive and read, releasing it with 'Z' when another device drives the bus?
questions.explanation: inout gives a bidirectional port that can be driven, released with 'Z' and read. buffer is an output that can be read back internally but cannot accept values from outside, and in and out work in one direction only.

questions.questionText: A signal is declared as integer range −100 to 100. How many bits does synthesis need to hold it in 2's complement?
questions.explanation: n bits of 2's complement cover −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1; 7 bits reach only −64 to 63, so 8 bits (−128 to 127) are needed, which GHDL --synth confirms. 201 is the number of values, not the number of bits.

questions.questionText: a, b and y are std_logic_vector(7 downto 0), and the design uses only ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. Which assignment compiles and adds a and b?
questions.explanation: numeric_std defines + for unsigned and signed but not for std_logic_vector, so a + b has no matching operator, and an unsigned sum cannot be assigned to a std_logic_vector without converting it back. GHDL analyses only the fully converted form.

options: Analysis fails because the lengths differ
Simulation stops with a length-mismatch error
questions.explanation: The predefined > on std_logic_vector compares elements from the left like strings: the first elements are both '1', then a's '0' is less than b's '1', so a < b and GHDL reports false. unsigned(a) > unsigned(b) compares 8 with 7 and gives TRUE.

questions.questionText: How many values does the std_ulogic type, on which std_logic is based, have?
questions.explanation: The nine values are 'U', 'X', '0', '1', 'Z', 'W', 'L', 'H' and '-'. The type bit has only two, '0' and '1'.

questions.questionText: With a = "1011" (a std_logic_vector(3 downto 0)), what is y after y <= a(2 downto 0) & a(3);?
questions.explanation: a(2 downto 0) is "011" and a(3) is '1', so the concatenation is "0111", a rotate left by one place (confirmed by GHDL). "1101" is the rotate right and "0110" is a shift left that fills with '0'.

questions.questionText: A testbench declares signal s : std_logic; with no initial value and never drives it. What value does a report of s show during simulation?
questions.explanation: Objects without an initial value start at the leftmost value of their type, and std_logic'left is 'U' (uninitialised); GHDL reports s='U'. 'X' appears only when drivers conflict or an operation involves unknown values.

questions.questionText:
What is the value of v after this declaration?

signal v : std_logic_vector(7 downto 0) := (6 => '1', 1 downto 0 => '1', others => '0');
questions.explanation: Named association sets bits 6, 1 and 0, and others fills the rest with '0'; with a downto range bit 7 is written first, giving "01000011" (x"43"), as GHDL reports. "11000010" is the same pattern read in reverse bit order.

questions.questionText: One concurrent statement drives an open-drain line with s <= 'H'; (the pull-up) and another drives s <= '0';. What is the resolved value of the std_logic signal s?
questions.explanation: The std_logic resolution function lets a forcing value override a weak one, so '0' wins over 'H'; GHDL reports '0'. 'X' results from '0' against '1', and 'W' from 'L' against 'H'.

The process runs once at time 0, giving y = '1' and '0' = '0', and is never resumed because b is missing from the sensitivity list, so y stays '0' (confirmed with GHDL). Synthesis would build an AND gate giving '1', a simulation-synthesis mismatch fixed by process (a, b) or process (all).

questions.questionText: Which std_logic value means "don't care", letting synthesis choose '0' or '1' for input combinations that never occur?
questions.explanation: '-' is the don't-care value. 'X' is forcing unknown (seen in simulation, e.g. after bus contention), 'U' is uninitialised and 'Z' is high impedance; note that v = "1-" is an exact comparison, and only the VHDL-2008 matching operator ?= treats '-' as a wildcard (GHDL: false and '1' for v = "10").

questions.questionText: Which of these processes is illegal in VHDL-2008?
options: process (clk) begin wait until clk = '1'; y <= a; end process;
process begin wait until clk = '1'; y <= a; end process;
process (all) begin y <= a and b; end process;
process (a, b) begin y <= a and b; end process;
questions.explanation: A process may have a sensitivity list or wait statements but not both; GHDL reports that a wait statement is not allowed in a sensitized process. process (all), new in VHDL-2008, makes the process sensitive to every signal it reads.

questions.questionText: Why is std_logic generally preferred over bit for signals in synthesisable designs and testbenches?
options: std_logic synthesises to fewer gates than bit
bit cannot be used in a port declaration
std_logic signals are updated without delta cycles
std_logic is resolved and can represent 'Z', 'X', 'U' and weak levels, so tri-state buses and uninitialised or conflicting signals can be simulated
questions.explanation: bit has only '0' and '1' and is unresolved, so it cannot show high impedance, contention or an uninitialised value. The synthesised hardware is the same; the benefit lies in modelling and simulation.

questions.questionText: An entity has the ports a : in std_logic; b : inout std_logic; y : out std_logic. Which statement in its architecture is illegal?
questions.explanation: A port of mode in can only be read, so the assignment to a is rejected (GHDL: port "a" can't be assigned). An inout port may be both driven and read, and an out port may be driven.

questions.questionText: a, b, c and y are std_logic signals. Which concurrent assignment fails to analyse?
options: y <= a and b and c;
y <= a and b or c;
questions.explanation: The binary logical operators all have the same precedence, and an unparenthesised sequence may repeat only one associative operator, so mixing and with or needs parentheses. not has higher precedence, so not a and b is legal and means (not a) and b.

questions.questionText:
Why does GHDL refuse to analyse this selected signal assignment, where sel is a std_logic_vector(1 downto 0)?

with sel select
  y <= a when "00",
       b when "01",
       c when "10",
       d when "11";
options: A selected signal assignment may only be used inside a process
The choices cover only 4 of the 81 possible values of sel, so a when others choice is required
The choices of a 2-bit selector must be written as integers
d when "11" repeats one of the earlier choices
questions.explanation: Each std_logic element has 9 values, so sel has 9² = 81 values, and a selected assignment, like a case statement, must cover all of them; GHDL reports missing choice(s). Changing the last choice to d when others makes it legal.

questions.questionText: Which of these statements can be written directly in an architecture body, outside any process?
options: if sel = '1' then y <= a; else y <= b; end if;
y <= a when sel = '1' else b;
case sel is when '1' => y <= a; when others => y <= b; end case;
for i in 0 to 3 loop y(i) <= a(i); end loop;
questions.explanation: The conditional signal assignment is a concurrent statement. if, case and loop are sequential statements that must sit inside a process or subprogram; outside a process GHDL tries to read them as generate statements, which need a label and the keyword generate.

questions.questionText: The integer signal m holds −7. What does integer'image(m / 2) report?
questions.explanation: VHDL integer division truncates toward zero, so −7/2 = −3, and GHDL reports -3. −4 would be floor division, and an integer result can never be −3.5.

questions.questionText: A signal is declared as signal d : std_logic_vector(15 downto 4);. What is d'length?
questions.explanation: 'length = high − low + 1 = 15 − 4 + 1 = 12, which GHDL reports. 11 forgets the + 1, and 16 and 15 wrongly assume the range starts at 0.

questions.questionText: Two concurrent signal assignments in an architecture are swapped so that the second one is written first. How does this change the simulated or synthesised behaviour?
options: The statement written last now takes priority
The design no longer compiles, because outputs must be assigned in port order
Not at all, because concurrent statements run whenever their inputs change, regardless of textual order
Only the simulation changes; synthesis still follows the original order
questions.explanation: Each concurrent statement behaves as an independent process sensitive to its inputs, so the order in which they appear in the architecture is irrelevant. Order matters only for sequential statements inside a process.
The generic map overrides the default of 8, so MAXV = 2^12 − 1 = 4095, as GHDL reports. 255 is the result for the default N = 8, 4096 forgets the − 1 and 2047 uses N − 1 = 11.

questions.questionText: What values do (−7) mod 3 and (−7) rem 3 give in VHDL?
questions.explanation: mod takes the sign of the right operand, so (−7) mod 3 = 2, while rem takes the sign of the left operand, so (−7) rem 3 = −1; GHDL reports 2 and -1. Without the parentheses −7 mod 3 would parse as −(7 mod 3) = −1.

questions.questionText: A memory type is declared as type mem_t is array (0 to 63) of std_logic_vector(31 downto 0);. How many bits of storage does one object of type mem_t represent?
questions.explanation: There are 64 elements of 32 bits each, so 64 × 32 = 2048 bits. 256 is the size in bytes, 2016 uses only 63 elements and 96 adds instead of multiplying.

questions.questionText: Entity sub has port (x : in integer; y : in integer; d : out integer) and computes d <= x - y;. Signals p = 3 and q = 10 are connected by u1 : entity work.sub port map (q, p, r);. What value does r take?
questions.explanation: Positional association connects the actuals to the formals in declaration order, x => q, y => p and d => r, so r = 10 − 3 = 7, which GHDL reports. Connecting p to x because p is declared first gives −7.
A variable is updated immediately, so the loop adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, which GHDL reports. The value 4 is what a signal assigned in the same loop would end up with.

questions.questionText: Which statement about y <= a after 5 ns; inside an RTL architecture is correct?
options: Synthesis inserts a 5 ns delay line in front of y
It is a syntax error in any architecture intended for synthesis
y changes immediately in simulation; the 5 ns is only a timing constraint for synthesis
In simulation y follows a 5 ns later, but synthesis ignores the after clause
questions.explanation: after clauses model delay for simulation only; synthesis tools ignore them, usually with a warning, because real delays come from the target technology. Timing requirements are given to the tools as separate constraints.

questions.questionText:
In VHDL-2008, what are the length and value of this constant?

constant C : std_logic_vector := 12X"3A";
questions.explanation: X"3A" is 0011 1010, and the prefix 12 sets the length, padding on the left with '0' because no S (signed) specifier is given; GHDL reports length 12 and 000000111010. Without the prefix the literal would be 8 bits long.

questions.questionText: A std_logic clock starts at 'U' and changes to '1' at 5 ns. In process (clk), which conditions are true at 5 ns?
questions.explanation: clk'event and clk = '1' only checks that clk changed and is now '1', whereas rising_edge(clk) also requires the previous value to be '0' or 'L'. A change from 'U' to '1' therefore satisfies only the first, and GHDL prints only the event-style message.

questions.questionText:
With s1 = '1' and s2 = '1', which input drives y?

y <= a when s1 = '1' else
     b when s2 = '1' else
     c;
options: a, because the first true condition wins
b, because the last true condition wins
None of them; y becomes 'X' because two conditions are true
questions.explanation: A conditional signal assignment tests its conditions in order and uses the first true one, which is why it synthesises to a priority multiplexer. The GHDL run with s1 = s2 = '1' gives y = a.

options: Simulation stops with a range (bound) check error, because −1 is outside natural
n becomes −1, because natural is just another name for integer
n stays 0 and the assignment is silently ignored
questions.explanation: natural is the subtype integer range 0 to integer'high, so n − 1 = −1 is a legal integer expression but assigning it to n fails the subtype check at run time; GHDL reports a bound check failure. VHDL integers never wrap around.

questions.questionText: With ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std in use, an entity has the port q : out unsigned(3 downto 0), and its clocked process contains q <= q + 1;. Which statement is correct?
options: It is legal in every VHDL version
It is illegal in VHDL-93 because an out port cannot be read, but legal in VHDL-2008
It is illegal in every VHDL version; q must be declared inout
It is legal only if q is changed to std_logic_vector
questions.explanation: GHDL with --std=93 reports that port q cannot be read, while --std=08 accepts the code, since VHDL-2008 allows out ports to be read inside the architecture. Before 2008 the usual fixes were an internal signal copied to the port, or mode buffer.

options: y1 stays '0'; y2 is '1' from 15 ns to 17 ns
Both are '1' from 15 ns to 17 ns
y1 is '1' from 15 ns to 17 ns; y2 stays '0'
questions.explanation: The default inertial delay rejects pulses shorter than the 5 ns delay, so the 2 ns pulse never reaches y1, while transport delay passes every pulse shifted by 5 ns. GHDL shows y2 rising at 15 ns and falling at 17 ns, with no event on y1.

small_t is a new type distinct from integer, so assigning it to z needs the explicit conversion integer(x). byte_t is only a subtype of integer, so z <= y and y <= z both analyse, the latter being range-checked at run time.

Variables keep their values between activations: the run at time 0 counts nothing, the run at 10 ns adds four ones (c = 4) and the run at 20 ns adds two more, so n = 6, as GHDL reports. Adding c := 0; at the top of the process would give 2.

subtopics.title: Overflow & Data Representation in VHDL
subtopics.subtitle: numeric_std types, conversions, wraparound, carry and signed overflow detection

concepts.text: Numbers Are Just Bit Patterns

A std_logic_vector is only a collection of bits with no numeric meaning. The standard package ieee.numeric_std adds two array types, unsigned (plain binary) and signed (2's complement), with arithmetic and comparison operators defined on them. The same bit pattern 1111 is 15 as unsigned and -1 as signed. The older std_logic_arith and std_logic_unsigned packages are vendor (Synopsys) packages, not IEEE standards, and should not be mixed with numeric_std.

rows: resize(x, m): zero-extends unsigned, sign-extends signed

concepts.text: Wraparound and Unsigned Overflow

In numeric_std, adding two n-bit unsigned values returns an n-bit result (the width of the larger operand), so any carry out of the MSB is silently discarded and the result wraps modulo 2^n. Unsigned overflow therefore means a carry out of the most significant bit. To capture it, extend the operands to n+1 bits with resize(a, n+1) or '0' & a before adding; the extra MSB of the sum is the carry.

concepts.plainText: S = (A + B) mod 2^n; Cout = 1 when A + B >= 2^n

concepts.text: Signed (2's Complement) Overflow

An n-bit signed value covers -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1, e.g. -128 to +127 for 8 bits. Overflow can occur only when both operands have the same sign and the result has the opposite sign; adding numbers of different signs can never overflow. Equivalently, overflow V is the XOR of the carry into the sign bit and the carry out of it. The carry out on its own means nothing for signed arithmetic.
Related representation issues:
items: Saturation vs wraparound: wraparound (default hardware behaviour) turns 127 + 1 into -128; saturating logic clamps to the maximum or minimum instead, preferred in DSP and audio.
Negation: -x = (not x) + 1; negating the most negative value (-128 in 8 bits) overflows back to -128.
Sign extension: resize on signed copies the MSB into the new bits (1010 becomes 11111010); on unsigned it fills with zeros.
integer vs unsigned: integer is at least 32-bit and has no wraparound; exceeding a declared range is a simulation error, whereas unsigned wraps silently.
Multiplication: an n-bit by m-bit product needs n + m bits, which numeric_std '*' returns automatically.

concepts.text: Fixed-point numbers store fractions in ordinary signed or unsigned vectors with an implied binary point. In Qm.f format there are m integer bits and f fraction bits, so the value is the integer reading divided by 2^f and the resolution is 2^-f. Adding requires aligned binary points; multiplying Qa.b by Qc.d gives a Q(a+c).(b+d) result that is usually truncated or rounded back. VHDL-2008 adds the ufixed and sfixed types in fixed_pkg for this purpose.
Worked Example: 4-bit 7 + 9

0111 + 1001 = 1 0000, with a carry generated at every bit position. Read as unsigned, 7 + 9 = 16 exceeds 15, so C_out = 1 and the 4-bit sum wraps to 0000; the add4 entity above would output sum = 0000, cout = '1'. Read as signed, 1001 is -7, so the operation is 7 + (-7) = 0: the operands have different signs, the carry into the MSB is 1 and the carry out is 1, so V = 1 XOR 1 = 0 and the result 0000 is correct.
Going Deeper: Widths, Overflow and Fixed Point

numeric_std never widens a sum on its own. For + and − the shorter operand is first extended (zero-extended for unsigned, sign-extended for signed) to the length of the longer one, and the result has that same length. An integer operand is converted to the vector's width with to_unsigned or to_signed, and a value that does not fit is truncated with a 'vector truncated' warning. Multiplication is the operator that grows: its result is as wide as both operands together, so a product can never overflow.

rows: Wraps modulo 2^8; the carry or borrow is lost
Sum of the widths; never overflows
a mod b, a rem b
One spare bit keeps the carry

concepts.latex: L(a \pm b) = \max(L_a, L_b), \quad L(a \times b) = L_a + L_b
concepts.plainText: len(a ± b) = max(La, Lb); len(a × b) = La + Lb

concepts.text: One spare bit is always enough to detect overflow. The sum of two n-bit signed numbers lies between −2^n and 2^n − 2, which fits in n + 1 bits, so sign-extending both operands to n + 1 bits makes the sum exact. The n-bit result is correct exactly when the top two bits of that exact sum are equal; if they differ, the n-bit result has overflowed. For unsigned operands the spare bit is simply the carry, and for a − b it is the borrow.

Worked example 1: 8-bit signed 100 + 50
a = +100  -> resize to 9 bits : 0 0110 0100
b =  +50  -> resize to 9 bits : 0 0011 0010
t = a + b (exact)              : 0 1001 0110 = +150
t(8) = 0, t(7) = 1  -> top two bits differ: overflow
wrapped 8-bit sum t(7 downto 0) = 1001 0110 = -106
sign-bit rule: a(7) = b(7) = 0 but s(7) = 1 -> V = 1
saturating output              : 0111 1111 = +127

-- a, b, y : signed(7 downto 0);  t : signed(8 downto 0)
t   <= resize(a, 9) + resize(b, 9);   -- exact sum, cannot overflow
ovf <= t(8) xor t(7);                  -- top two bits differ
y   <= "01111111" when t(8) = '0' and t(7) = '1' else   -- clamp at +127
       "10000000" when t(8) = '1' and t(7) = '0' else   -- clamp at -128
       t(7 downto 0);
-- simulated: (100, 50) -> y = 127, ovf = '1';  (-100, -50) -> y = -128, ovf = '1'
--            (100, -50) -> y = 50, ovf = '0';  (-128, -1) -> y = -128, ovf = '1'

Fixed-point multiplication needs one more bookkeeping step. If a and b are n-bit signed vectors with f fraction bits each, their 2n-bit product has 2f fraction bits. To return to n bits with f fraction bits, drop the lowest f bits and keep the next n, which is the slice p(n + f − 1 downto f). The bits above that slice must all equal its sign bit; otherwise the true result is out of range and should be saturated.

Worked example 2: 8-bit signed, 4 fraction bits (value = N / 16)
a = 0010 1000 ->  40 / 16 =  2.5
b = 1110 1100 -> -20 / 16 = -1.25
p = a * b (16 bits, 8 fraction bits) = -800 -> -800 / 256 = -3.125
p = 1111 1100 1110 0000
keep p(11 downto 4) = 1100 1110 = -50 -> -50 / 16 = -3.125
p(15 downto 11) = 11111 (all equal to the sign) -> no overflow
wrong slice p(7 downto 0) = 1110 0000 = -32 -> -2.0
Simulation behaviour that often surprises:
items: to_integer on a vector containing 'U', 'X', 'Z', 'W' or '-' returns 0 with a metavalue warning, while +, − and * return a vector of all 'X'.
A counter with no reset and no initial value starts at "UUUU", and cnt + 1 keeps it at "XXXX" for the whole run.
to_unsigned(300, 8) and to_signed(200, 8) keep only the low 8 bits (44 and −56) and print 'vector truncated'; to_unsigned(−1, 8) is a bound-check error because its argument is of subtype natural.
Assigning a result to a target of a different length is a run-time bound-check failure, never a silent truncation.
An integer subtype such as range 0 to 15 stops the simulation when it reaches 16, whereas unsigned(3 downto 0) wraps to 0 like the hardware.
Shrinking with resize keeps the low bits of an unsigned value, but for a signed value it keeps the sign bit plus the low bits.

concepts.text: Size first, then operate: widen the operands before + or − when you need the carry or the overflow flag, remember that * returns the sum of the widths, and use resize or a slice to fit a target, because a width mismatch on assignment stops the simulation instead of truncating.

notes.text: numeric_std '+' does not widen its result: unsigned(3 downto 0) + unsigned(3 downto 0) is 4 bits, so the carry is lost unless you resize the operands to n+1 bits first.
Signed overflow rule: same-sign operands and a result of the opposite sign. Unsigned overflow: carry out of the MSB. Different-sign signed addition never overflows.
Use ieee.numeric_std for arithmetic; do not combine it with the non-standard std_logic_arith or std_logic_unsigned packages in the same unit.

flashcards.front: How do you detect unsigned overflow when adding two n-bit unsigned values in VHDL?
flashcards.back: Resize both operands to n+1 bits before adding; the MSB of the (n+1)-bit sum is the carry out, which signals overflow.
When both operands have the same sign and the result has the opposite sign, i.e. V = carry into MSB XOR carry out of MSB.

flashcards.front: What does resize do to signed and unsigned values?
flashcards.back: It sign-extends signed values (copies the MSB) and zero-extends unsigned values; when shrinking it drops upper bits.

questions.questionText: Two 4-bit signed (2's complement) values 0110 and 0101 are added. What is the 4-bit result and is there overflow?
questions.explanation: 6 + 5 = 11 exceeds +7. Both operands are positive but the result 1011 is negative, so signed overflow occurs; the carry out is 0.

questions.questionText: Which ieee.numeric_std function converts an integer i into an 8-bit unsigned value?
questions.explanation: to_unsigned(i, n) takes the value and the width. A type cast such as unsigned(i) works only between closely related array types, not from integer.

questions.questionText: With ieee.numeric_std, a and b are unsigned(7 downto 0). What is the width of a + b?
options: 8 bits, so a carry out of the MSB is lost
questions.explanation: numeric_std addition returns the width of the larger operand, so the sum wraps modulo 256. Resize to 9 bits to keep the carry.

questions.questionText: What is resize(signed'("1010"), 8)?
questions.explanation: resize on a signed value sign-extends by copying the MSB (1), so -6 in 4 bits becomes 11111010, which is -6 in 8 bits.

questions.questionText: Which IEEE-standard VHDL package defines the array types signed and unsigned together with arithmetic and comparison operators for them?
questions.explanation: numeric_std (originally IEEE 1076.3, now part of IEEE 1076-2008) defines signed and unsigned. std_logic_arith and std_logic_unsigned are Synopsys packages, not IEEE standards, and std_logic_1164 defines only the std_logic types.

questions.questionText: u is a signal of type unsigned(7 downto 0). What does the expression std_logic_vector(u) do?
options: It converts u to 2's complement by inverting the bits and adding 1
It relabels the same 8 bits as a std_logic_vector, so no logic is generated
It adds a sign bit, giving a 9-bit vector
It converts u into two BCD digits
questions.explanation: unsigned and std_logic_vector are closely related array types with the same element type, so this type conversion keeps every bit unchanged and costs no hardware.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. What bit pattern does std_logic_vector(to_signed(-3, 6)) produce?
questions.explanation: to_signed gives the 6-bit 2's complement of −3: 2^6 − 3 = 61 = 111101. 100011 is sign-magnitude, 111100 is 1's complement and 000011 is +3.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. v is a std_logic_vector(7 downto 0) initialised to x"EC". What are to_integer(unsigned(v)) and to_integer(signed(v))?
questions.explanation: EC = 1110 1100 = 236 read as unsigned. Read as 2's complement it is 236 − 256 = −20; −108 comes from misreading the pattern as sign-magnitude.

questions.questionText: A design uses only ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. v is a std_logic_vector(7 downto 0) holding an unsigned number and n is an integer. Which assignment analyses and sets n to the value of v?
questions.explanation: numeric_std's to_integer accepts signed or unsigned, so v must first be converted to unsigned. integer(v) is not a legal type conversion from an array type, and conv_integer belongs to the Synopsys packages, which are not used here.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. s is signed(7 downto 0) holding −3, u is unsigned(3 downto 0) holding "1100" (12) and r is signed(7 downto 0). Which assignment is legal and makes r = 9?
questions.explanation: Prefixing '0' turns 12 into the 5-bit positive signed number 01100, so r = −3 + 12 = 9. signed(u) reads 1100 as −4 (giving −7), numeric_std has no + for a signed and an unsigned operand, and unsigned(s) + u is unsigned, which cannot be assigned to the signed r.

questions.questionText: What are resize(unsigned'("10110110"), 4) and resize(signed'("10110110"), 4) in ieee.numeric_std?
questions.explanation: Shrinking an unsigned value keeps the rightmost bits (0110). Shrinking a signed value keeps the sign bit and the rightmost 3 bits, giving 1 & 110 = 1110, so the result stays negative even though its value changes.

questions.questionText: Which ieee.numeric_std function changes the width of a signed value while keeping its numeric value, provided the new width is large enough?
questions.explanation: resize(x, n) sign-extends a signed value (or zero-extends an unsigned one) to n bits. to_signed converts an integer, std_logic_vector only changes the type, and shift_left moves the bits and so changes the value.

questions.questionText: What does to_signed(200, 8) return in an ieee.numeric_std simulation?
options: Nothing, because the simulation stops with a range error
questions.explanation: +200 needs 9 bits as a signed number. to_signed keeps the low 8 bits, 1100 1000, which reads as 200 − 256 = −56, and numeric_std only prints a warning.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. n is an integer signal holding −1 and u is unsigned(7 downto 0). What happens in simulation when u <= to_unsigned(n, 8); executes?
options: A bound (range) check error stops the simulation, because the first parameter of to_unsigned is of subtype natural
u becomes "XXXXXXXX" and a warning is printed
questions.explanation: to_unsigned is declared with an argument of subtype natural, so passing −1 violates the subtype and the simulator reports a bound-check failure. Use to_signed for values that can be negative.

The upper nibble 1001 read as signed is −7 and the lower nibble 1100 read as unsigned is 12, so n = −7 + 12 = 5. 21 reads both nibbles as unsigned, while −100 and 156 are the whole byte read as signed and unsigned.

questions.questionText: What range of values can a signal declared as signed(5 downto 0) hold?
questions.explanation: signed(5 downto 0) has 6 bits, so its 2's complement range is −2^5 to 2^5 − 1 = −32 to +31. −31 to +31 is the sign-magnitude range, 0 to 63 the unsigned range, and −64 to +63 would need 7 bits.

questions.questionText: An internal signal must hold a 12-bit two's-complement sample that is added to and compared with other samples. Which declaration expresses this with ieee.numeric_std?
questions.explanation: signed gives the bits a 2's complement meaning, and numeric_std defines arithmetic and comparison on it. unsigned and integer range 0 to 4095 cannot hold negative values, and std_logic_vector has no numeric meaning in numeric_std.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. a is unsigned(7 downto 0) and b is unsigned(3 downto 0). What are the widths of a + b and a * b?
questions.explanation: Addition returns the width of the longer operand (8 bits), with b zero-extended first, so a carry out is lost. Multiplication returns the sum of the widths, 8 + 4 = 12 bits.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. A variable u : unsigned(3 downto 0) holds "0000". What does it hold after u := u - 1;?
options: "0000", because unsigned arithmetic saturates at zero
Nothing, because the simulation stops with a range error
questions.explanation: numeric_std arithmetic wraps silently: 0 − 1 = −1 ≡ 15 (mod 2^4), which is 1111. Vector arithmetic never saturates or raises an error.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. a = 23 and b = 45 are of type unsigned(7 downto 0), and y is unsigned(7 downto 0). Which concurrent assignment is legal and gives y the low 8 bits of the full product (1035)?
questions.explanation: resize on an unsigned value keeps the low 8 bits: 1035 mod 256 = 11. A parenthesised expression cannot be sliced, the nibble product 7 × 13 = 91 is a different number, and the 16-bit a * b does not match the 8-bit target, so simulation stops with a bound-check error.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. a and b are unsigned(7 downto 0), both equal to 200, and sum9 is unsigned(8 downto 0). Which concurrent assignment makes sum9 equal to 400?
questions.explanation: Widening a before the addition makes the + 9 bits wide (b is zero-extended), so the carry is kept and the sum is 400. Resizing or concatenating after an 8-bit addition keeps the wrapped value 400 − 256 = 144, and the 8-bit a + b does not match the 9-bit target, so simulation stops with a bound-check error.

questions.questionText: In ieee.numeric_std each operator sets its own result width. Which operation on two unsigned operands can never lose significant bits?
questions.explanation: The product of an n-bit and an m-bit operand is returned with n + m bits, which always holds the full result. Addition and subtraction return the width of the wider operand, so a carry or borrow is dropped and the result wraps.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. a and b are signed(3 downto 0) and both hold "1000". p is signed(7 downto 0) and p <= a * b;. What is to_integer(p)?
questions.explanation: Each operand is −8, so the product is +64. numeric_std returns a 4 + 4 = 8-bit product, and 0100 0000 = +64 fits in the signed 8-bit range, so even the most negative operands cannot overflow the full-width product.

questions.questionText: Which statement about ieee.numeric_std is NOT correct?
options: a + b on two unsigned operands returns the width of the wider operand
resize on a signed operand fills the new upper bits with copies of the sign bit
to_integer applied to an unsigned argument returns a value of subtype natural
a * b returns the width of the wider operand, so the upper half of the product is lost
questions.explanation: A product has as many bits as both operands together (n + m), so no bits are lost. The other three statements are true.

The 9-bit sum is 290 = 1 0010 0010, so t(8) = '1' flags the unsigned overflow and the low byte is 290 − 256 = 34. Adding the carry back in (35) is 1's complement practice, and 255 is what a saturating adder would give.

options: "00010"; d5(4) = '0' because the magnitude of the difference is 2
"11110"; d5(4) = '1' is a borrow, showing that a < b
"10010"; d5(4) = '1' is the sign bit of −2 in sign-magnitude form
questions.explanation: The 5-bit difference is 3 − 5 = −2 ≡ 30 = 11110 (mod 32). The low 4 bits, 1110 = 14, are the wrapped 4-bit result, and the extra MSB is 1 exactly when a borrow occurs, i.e. when a < b.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. a, b and s are unsigned(7 downto 0) and s <= a + b;, so the carry is lost. Which expression, using only the most significant bits, recovers the carry out?
options: cout <= (a(7) and b(7)) or ((a(7) or b(7)) and not s(7));
cout <= (a(7) xnor b(7)) and (s(7) xor a(7));
cout <= (a(7) or b(7)) and not s(7);
questions.explanation: The carry out of bit 7 is a7·b7 + (a7 ⊕ b7)·c7, and when exactly one of a7, b7 is 1, s7 = not c7. The second option is the signed-overflow test, a(7) and b(7) misses carries such as 192 + 64, and the last misses cases such as 192 + 192 where s7 = 1; an exhaustive simulation of all 65,536 pairs confirms only the first.
The true sum −150 is below −128, so it wraps to −150 + 256 = +106 (−150 cannot be held in 8 bits). Both operands are negative and the result's sign bit differs from a(7), so ovf = '1'.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. a, b and d are signed(3 downto 0) and d <= a - b;. Which expression gives ovf = '1' exactly when the subtraction overflows?
options: ovf <= (a(3) xnor b(3)) and (d(3) xor a(3));
ovf <= (a(3) xor b(3)) and (d(3) xor b(3));
ovf <= (a(3) xor b(3)) and (d(3) xor a(3));
questions.explanation: a − b can overflow only when a and b have different signs, and it has overflowed when the result's sign differs from a's. The first option is the addition rule, the second compares the result with the wrong operand, and the third also fires for correct results such as 1 − 2 = −1; checking all 256 operand pairs confirms only the last.

The exact 9-bit sums are +150 = 0 1001 0110 and −150 = 1 0110 1010. In both the top two bits differ, so an 8-bit result would overflow; the circuit saturates to +127 and −128 instead of wrapping to −106 and +106.
acc goes 60, 120 and then 120 + 60 = 180, which wraps to 180 − 256 = −76. On the third edge a non-negative acc produced a negative sum, so the sticky flag ovf is set to '1'.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. a is signed(3 downto 0) := "1000". What is to_integer(abs a)?
questions.explanation: abs returns a 4-bit result, and +8 does not fit in the 4-bit range −8 to +7. Negating 1000 gives 0111 + 1 = 1000 again, so the result is still −8.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. v is std_logic_vector(7 downto 0) := x"90". What are to_integer(shift_right(signed(v), 2)) and to_integer(shift_right(unsigned(v), 2))?
questions.explanation: x"90" is −112 as signed and 144 as unsigned. shift_right on a signed value copies the sign bit (1110 0100 = −28 = −112/4), while on an unsigned value it fills with zeros (0010 0100 = 36 = 144/4).

questions.questionText: Up to VHDL-2008, what is the smallest range that the predefined type integer is guaranteed to cover in every implementation?
questions.explanation: The language standard requires integer to include at least −(2^31 − 1) to +(2^31 − 1); most tools, GHDL included, implement the 32-bit 2's complement range −2^31 to 2^31 − 1.

questions.questionText: In two separate designs, counter A is unsigned(3 downto 0) (ieee.numeric_std) and counter B is integer range 0 to 15. Each holds 15, and at the next rising edge its clocked process executes A <= A + 1; or B <= B + 1; respectively. What happens in simulation?
options: A wraps to "0000", while B raises a bound-check error that stops the simulation
Both designs stop with a range error
A stops with a range error, while B wraps to 0
questions.explanation: numeric_std vector arithmetic wraps modulo 2^4, so A becomes 0000. An integer subtype has no wraparound, so assigning 16 to B is outside 0 to 15 and is a bound-check failure; the synthesised 4-bit hardware would simply wrap.

questions.questionText: Which package, added to the IEEE library in VHDL-2008, lets you write arithmetic such as v + 1 directly on a std_logic_vector, treating it as an unsigned number?
questions.explanation: numeric_std_unsigned overloads the arithmetic and relational operators for std_logic_vector with an unsigned meaning. numeric_bit works on bit vectors, math_real on type real and fixed_pkg on ufixed and sfixed.

questions.questionText: An unsigned(7 downto 0) signal stores a fixed-point number with 4 integer bits and 4 fraction bits (value = stored integer / 16). It holds "10011000". What value does it represent?
questions.explanation: The stored integer is 152 and 152 / 2^4 = 9.5 (1001.1000 in binary). 152 ignores the binary point, and 4.75 and 19.0 put it in the wrong place.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. Two signed(7 downto 0) signals hold fixed-point values with 4 fraction bits (value = stored integer / 16): a = "00101100" and b = "11101000". What value does s <= a + b; represent?
questions.explanation: a = 44/16 = 2.75 and b = −24/16 = −1.5. Both have the same binary point, so the integer sum 20 has 4 fraction bits too: 20/16 = 1.25. Taking b as +1.5 gives 4.25, forgetting the scale gives 20, and a sign-magnitude reading of b gives −3.75.

questions.questionText: Two numbers are held in plain signed vectors, x with 4 fraction bits and y with 6 fraction bits. What must be done before adding them with an ordinary integer adder?
options: Align the binary points first, for example widen x and shift it left by 2 places so both have 6 fraction bits
Nothing, because the stored integers can be added directly
Add the stored integers and shift the sum right by 2 afterwards
Convert both to unsigned so that the sign bits are ignored
questions.explanation: Bits can only be added when they have equal weight, so both operands need the same number of fraction bits. Adding unaligned integers, or shifting after the addition, mixes weights of 2^−4 and 2^−6 and gives a wrong result.

questions.questionText: 0.3 is to be stored in an unsigned(7 downto 0) as a fraction with 8 fraction bits (value = N / 256), rounding to the nearest code. What are N and the value actually stored?
questions.explanation: 0.3 × 256 = 76.8, which rounds to 77, and 77/256 = 0.30078125 (an error of about 0.0008). Truncation gives 76, 30 treats the scale as decimal, and 154 uses 2^9 instead of 2^8.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. a and b are signed(7 downto 0) with 4 fraction bits (value = stored integer / 16): a = "00101000" (2.5) and b = "11101100" (−1.25). p <= a * b; is signed(15 downto 0) with 8 fraction bits. Which slice of p gives the product back as 8 bits with 4 fraction bits, and what value does it represent?
questions.explanation: The integer product is 40 × (−20) = −800, i.e. −800/256 = −3.125. Dropping the 4 extra fraction bits and keeping 8 bits selects p(11 downto 4) = −50, and −50/16 = −3.125; bits 15 to 11 all equal the sign, so the value is in range. −50 is the stored integer, not the value.

questions.questionText: With the VHDL-2008 package ieee.fixed_pkg, a signal is declared as sfixed(3 downto -4). What are its width and its range of values?
questions.explanation: Indices 3 down to −4 give 8 bits; the negative indices are fraction bits, so the LSB weighs 2^−4 = 0.0625. As a signed number the range is −2^3 to 2^3 − 2^−4 = −8 to +7.9375, while 0 to 15.9375 would be the ufixed range.

questions.questionText: With the default settings of the VHDL-2008 package ieee.fixed_pkg (round to nearest, saturate on overflow), what value does to_sfixed(9.3, 3, -4) produce?
questions.explanation: sfixed(3 downto −4) can hold at most 7.9375, so the default overflow style saturates to that value and prints a warning. Wrapping the rounded code 149 into 8 bits would give −107/16 = −6.6875, 9.3125 is not representable, and 1.3125 drops the integer bit worth 8.

questions.questionText: With the VHDL-2008 package ieee.fixed_pkg, a and b are ufixed(3 downto -2). What index ranges do the results of a + b and a * b have?
questions.explanation: Unlike numeric_std, fixed_pkg sizes results so that they cannot overflow: a sum gains one integer bit, (3 + 1 downto −2), and a product adds the ranges, (3 + 3 + 1 downto −2 + −2) = (7 downto −4).

questions.questionText: Two concurrent statements drive the same std_logic signal r, one with r <= '0'; and the other with r <= '1';. What value does r have in simulation?
questions.explanation: The std_logic resolution function combines a forcing 0 and a forcing 1 into 'X' (forcing unknown), which models bus contention.
With both drivers at 'Z' the line floats ('Z'); one driver at '0' against 'Z' resolves to '0'; '0' against '1' is contention and resolves to 'X'.

questions.questionText: Using the ieee.std_logic_1164 operators, what are the results of '0' and 'X', '1' and 'X', and not 'Z'?
questions.explanation: A 0 input forces an AND gate to 0 whatever the other input is, so '0' and 'X' = '0', while '1' and 'X' stays unknown. The logic tables treat 'Z' as an unknown input, so not 'Z' = 'X'.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008. An architecture contains the two concurrent assignments y <= a; and y <= b;, where a, b and y all have the same type. For which type of y is this illegal?
questions.explanation: std_ulogic is unresolved, so a signal of that type may have only one driver and elaboration fails. std_logic, std_logic_vector and (in VHDL-2008) numeric_std's unsigned are resolved, so their drivers are combined by the resolution function.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. cnt is declared as signal cnt : unsigned(3 downto 0); with no initial value, and its clocked process contains only cnt <= cnt + 1; inside if rising_edge(clk) then, with no reset. What does simulation show for cnt after three rising edges?
questions.explanation: cnt starts at "UUUU" (the leftmost std_logic value). numeric_std's + returns all 'X' when an operand contains a metavalue, so the counter shows XXXX from the first edge onward; it needs a reset or an initial value.

questions.questionText: Assume VHDL-2008 with ieee.std_logic_1164 and ieee.numeric_std. u is unsigned(3 downto 0) and holds "10X1". What does to_integer(u) return in simulation?
options: Nothing, because the simulation stops with a fatal error
questions.explanation: to_integer cannot interpret 'X', so numeric_std prints a warning and returns 0. It does not guess 9 or 11, and the assertion has severity warning, so the simulation continues.

subtopics.title: Combinational & Sequential Logic Design in VHDL
subtopics.subtitle: Concurrent statements, clocked processes, registers, counters and FSM coding

concepts.text: Concurrent Statements for Combinational Logic

Statements written directly in an architecture body are concurrent: they all run in parallel and their order in the file does not matter. Each concurrent assignment behaves like a small process that re-evaluates whenever a signal on its right-hand side changes, which is exactly how combinational gates behave. Combinational logic such as AND/OR networks, multiplexers, decoders, adders and comparators is usually written this way.
Concurrent statement forms and typical circuits:
items: Simple assignment: y <= (a and b) or c; full adder: s <= a xor b xor cin; cout <= (a and b) or (cin and (a xor b));
Conditional assignment (when-else): has priority, like a chain of 2:1 muxes; used for priority encoders and decoders.
Selected assignment (with-select): one choice per value, like a true multiplexer; all choices must be covered, usually with others.
Comparator: gt <= '1' when a > b else '0'; with a, b of type unsigned.
for-generate replicates hardware (e.g. n full adders); if-generate includes hardware conditionally from a generic.

concepts.text:
-- 4-to-1 multiplexer (selected assignment)
with sel select
  y <= d0 when "00",
       d1 when "01",
       d2 when "10",
       d3 when others;
-- 2-to-4 decoder with enable (conditional assignment)
dec <= "0001" when en = '1' and a = "00" else
       "0010" when en = '1' and a = "01" else
       "0100" when en = '1' and a = "10" else
       "1000" when en = '1' else
       "0000";

Combinational logic can also be written as a process, but its sensitivity list must contain every signal read inside it (VHDL-2008 allows process (all)), and every output must be assigned on every path through the code. If some path leaves an output unassigned, the output must remember its old value, and synthesis infers a latch, which is almost never intended. Assign default values at the top of the process or cover every if/case branch.
Sequential Logic with Clocked Processes

Sequential logic is written as a process triggered by the clock. Inside, if rising_edge(clk) (or the older clk'event and clk = '1') marks the active edge, and every signal assigned under it becomes a flip-flop. A synchronous reset is tested inside the clock-edge branch, so only clk is in the sensitivity list; an asynchronous reset appears in the sensitivity list and is tested before the clock edge.

rows: At the next active clock edge
Filters reset glitches; needs a running clock
Works without a clock; release must be synchronised

concepts.text: Other common sequential blocks:
items: Register: a vector of D flip-flops, e.g. if en = '1' then r <= d; end if; inside the clocked branch.
Shift register: sr <= sr(2 downto 0) & din; shifts left by one bit each clock using concatenation.
Mod-N counter: reset the count to zero when it reaches N - 1 instead of letting it wrap at 2^n.
Clock divider: the MSB of an n-bit free-running counter toggles at f_clk / 2^n.

concepts.text: Finite State Machines

An FSM is coded with an enumerated state type, a clocked process holding the state register, and a case statement for next-state logic. In a Moore machine outputs depend only on the current state, so they change one clock after the input and are glitch-free. In a Mealy machine outputs depend on the state and the current inputs, so they react in the same cycle and often need fewer states. Synthesis chooses binary, Gray or one-hot state encoding.

concepts.plainText: flip-flops = ceil(log2 N) for binary encoding, N for one-hot

concepts.text: Going Deeper: From VHDL Code to Gates and Flip-Flops

Synthesis reads a process by asking, for every signal, when it is assigned. A signal assigned under if rising_edge(clk) becomes a flip-flop, one per bit, and all right-hand sides in that branch use the values from before the edge. In a combinational process, a signal that some path leaves unassigned must keep its value, so a latch is built. Within one run of a process the last assignment to a signal wins, which makes a default assignment at the top a simple way to cover every path.

rows: y <= a when s = '1' else b;
Choices are exclusive and must cover every value, usually with others
case in process (all), every output assigned
A path without an assignment gives a latch
rst must be in the sensitivity list
if en = '1' inside the clock branch
Not a latch: the flip-flop holds the value
Shifts left one place per edge

concepts.text:
Simulated trace (x changes just after each edge; cycle k lies between edges k and k+1)
cycle        :  1    2    3     4     5     6
x            :  1    0    1     0     1     1
Moore state  :  S0   S1   S10   S101  S10   S101
z_moore      :  0    0    0     1     0     1
z_mealy      :  0    0    1     0     1     0

The trace shows the defining difference between the two machines. The Mealy detector needs only the states none, 1 and 10, and raises z as soon as the final 1 is on its input, in cycles 3 and 5. The Moore detector needs a fourth state, 101 seen, and its output appears only after the edge that enters that state, one cycle later in cycles 4 and 6. Because the Moore output comes from the state register it is not disturbed by input changes, whereas input glitches pass straight through to a Mealy output.

rows: One clock after the input is sampled
In the same cycle as the input
z <= '1' when st = M10 and x = '1' else '0';

concepts.plainText: f_tick = f_clk / N; bits = ceil(log2 N) for a counter that counts 0 to N - 1

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: 1 kHz tick from a 50 MHz clock
N       = f_clk / f_tick = 50,000,000 / 1,000 = 50,000 states (count 0 .. 49,999)
bits    = ceil(log2 50,000) = 16   (2^15 = 32,768 < 50,000 <= 65,536 = 2^16)
tick    = '1' for one clock when cnt = N - 1 = 49,999
check   : 50 MHz / 50,000 = 1 kHz, pulse width 1 / 50 MHz = 20 ns
mistake : comparing with N gives N + 1 states -> 50e6 / 50,001 = 999.98 Hz
simulated with N = 6 and a 10 ns clock: tick every 60 ns; compare-with-N version every 70 ns
Mistakes that make the hardware differ from what was intended:
items: An output left unassigned on some path of a combinational process: a latch is inferred.
Reset tested before rising_edge(clk) but missing from the sensitivity list: simulation resets only at the next clock event, while the hardware resets at once.
A synchronous reset pulse shorter than a clock period can fall between two edges and be missed completely.
Comparing a counter with N instead of N − 1: the counter has N + 1 states.
Signals where variables were intended, or the reverse, in a clocked process: the number of register stages changes.
An else branch after if rising_edge(clk): no flip-flop can implement it, so synthesis rejects it or builds no register.

concepts.text: To trace a clocked process, read every right-hand side with the values from before the edge, let the last assignment to each signal win, and update all signals together at the end; only variables change immediately.

formulas.plainText: n_FF = ceil(log2 N) flip-flops for N binary-encoded states
f_MSB = f_clk / 2^n for an n-bit counter
an n-bit binary counter counts 0 to 2^n - 1 (modulus 2^n)

notes.text: An incomplete if or case in a combinational process (an output not assigned on some path) infers a latch. Give every output a default value or cover every branch, and keep the sensitivity list complete.

Concurrent assignments (when-else, with-select) model combinational logic; a process with rising_edge(clk) models flip-flops, registers, counters and FSMs. Moore: outputs from state only; Mealy: outputs from state and inputs.

A testbench is an entity with no ports that instantiates the design under test, generates a clock (clk <= not clk after 5 ns;), applies stimulus with wait statements and checks outputs with assert. It is for simulation only and is not synthesised.
